[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday "simulate" suggests replaying a known process to get its answer; here each run of RandomSurfer draws fresh random numbers and gives different estimates (100 moves: 0.24 0.23 0.16 0.25 0.12), which only approach the page ranks as T grows.
[1] misconception (M) -> OffByOneBound: wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: for (int t = 0; t < T; t++) makes exactly T moves; with <= it makes T + 1, while the ranks are still divided by T.
[2] misconception (M) -> FewTrialsAreExact: wrong rule: A short simulation gives the exact page ranks. Right rule: A simulation only estimates the ranks: about 10^n moves for n-digit precision, tens of thousands of moves for two accurate places and millions for three.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> OffByOneBound: Applies LT (draw r, find next page, then freq[page]++) unevenly: e.g. counting the current page before the move on some passes, or resetting sum only on the first pass. (here mixing in: "< vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable")
[4] misconception (M) -> LoopBodyScopeImpliesLoopLifetime: wrong rule: A variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations. Right rule: r and sum are declared inside the t-loop body and are created anew on every move; freq and page must be declared before the loop to persist.

[0] names_the_element (N): A Monte Carlo simulation: a for loop over t = 0..T-1 that makes one random move per pass and tallies the page reached.
[1] states_the_rule (S): RandomSurfer reads a transition matrix, starts at page 0, makes T moves (T from the command line) according to the matrix, and counts the visits to each page.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Per pass: r = Math.random(); sum = 0.0; inner j loop picks the next page; freq[page]++; t++ and test t < T. After the loop, each freq[i] is divided by T and printed.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Prints N doubles (%8.5f) that sum to about 1 and vary between runs; 1,000,000 moves on tiny.txt gave 0.27324 0.26568 0.14581 0.24737 0.06790.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One pass changes page (to the next page) and increases freq[page] by 1; t increases by 1.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The loop body is one random move; page carries state from one pass to the next, so each move uses the row of the page reached last.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): freq[page]++ must come after the move and inside the loop, once per pass, so the counts total T.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): A counted for loop with t < T fixes the number of moves at T; the loop variable t is scoped to the loop.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): Both compute the same page ranks; the power method gets them exactly with far fewer iterations.
[4] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Monte Carlo estimation plan: repeat a random experiment many times and count outcomes; t is a stepper, page a most-recent holder, freq[] the per-page gatherers.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> OffByOneBound: Changing the start page keeps the limit (mixing); increasing T keeps the estimates but makes them more accurate (about 10x moves per extra digit); changing < to <= or the division by T breaks the normalisation.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use when the process is easy to simulate and a rough estimate suffices (or no matrix is available); not for accurate ranks or large models, where a huge number of trials is needed and the power method is far more efficient.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Loop must run t = 0..T-1. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: t <= T makes T+1 moves but ranks are divided by T, so they sum to slightly more than 1.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A variable declared in the body is recreated each pass. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: int[] freq = new int[N] declared inside the loop body: counts reset every move (and freq is out of scope after the loop, a compile-time error if printed there).
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: freq[i] / T must be floating-point division. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Printing freq[i] / T without the (double) cast: every rank prints as 0 (or 1).
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The number of moves is args[0]. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: Run without a command-line argument: args[0] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; a non-numeric argument makes Integer.parseInt throw NumberFormatException.

The power method used in Markov is far more efficient than simulating the behavior of a random surfer.
The simulation is a for loop over t = 0 ... T - 1 that makes one random move per pass.
The simulation repeats the random move T times, each move starting from the page the previous move reached.
On each pass the simulation adds 1 to freq[page] for the page just reached.
